items.title: Evolution of Anxiety, Fear, and Behavior Evaluation Scales for Pediatric Dental Patients: A Comprehensive Review of Literature
items.abstract: Anxiety and fear are generally the reactions to stressful circumstances. The underlying dental anxiety, fear, or phobia usually makes the kids’ behavior uncooperative, i.e., maladaptive behavior in the context of dentistry, and thereby the needed dental treatment or intervention becomes challenging or difficult for the pedodontist or general dentist. A proper analysis of the behavior, anxiety, and fear, as well as their cooperative potential in pediatric patients, is considered crucial to aid the clinician in proper treatment planning and to make the dental visits more efficient and effective in terms of the delivery of optimal dental care. Hence, the knowledge and selection of the suitable methods or ways for the determination of the status of anxiety, fear, and behavior of pediatric patient is considered pivotal for dental clinicians in providing the optimal dental care with favorable behavior management in clinical settings. There are numerous conventional assessment methods, and furthermore, recently some newer modern scales/tools for anxiety/behavior evaluation have been reported in recent years. The objective of the current review was to explore, unveil and describe the different tools/modalities for kids’ behavior, anxiety and fear assessment. This is a narrative review article. The literature was searched from scientific databases, namely,. “PubMed/Medline,” “Scopus,” “Web of Science,” “DOAJ,” “Lilacs,” ScienceDirect and “Scielo,” Google Scholar, along with manual searching methods. This article provides an overview of the traditional as well as the recently reported modern scales/tools (e.g., digital or artificial intelligence-based methods) for the anxiety, fear, and behavior assessment. The newly reported anxiety, fear, and behavior assessment tools/modalities have been reported to be promising or favorable in contemporary pediatric dentistry.

items.title: Executive function and task engagement in workload and mental fatigue: a multi-domain study using a novel adaptive paradigm
items.abstract: This experimental study investigated how perceived workload is influenced by executive function load (lower, higher) and task engagement (via non-adaptive or adaptive task pacing), across the three domains of inhibition, switching, and updating. It further explored how mental fatigue develops from sustained performance under varying levels of these factors. Seventy-two adults were randomly allocated to three groups, each completing six tasks at an individualised pace and in a distinct combination of executive function load and task engagement. Workload was not altered by executive function load, but it increased significantly under adaptive pacing, with the most pronounced effect in the inhibition domain. Mental fatigue emerged across all conditions regardless of workload differences, but its onset was anticipated under low executive function load with non-adaptive pacing and under high executive function load with adaptive pacing. These findings suggest that under- and over-stimulation may be two different paths to mental fatigue.

items.title: Expanded Coverage Mistaken for an Unpositioned View: Why a Wider View Still Comes From Somewhere
items.abstract: This conceptual paper introduces Expanded Coverage Mistaken for an Unpositioned View, a mechanism by which increasing the coverage of an inquiry can lead its users to overlook the position, boundaries, and selections that still govern what it shows. A view can extend across many places or observations without escaping the conditions under which those observations were produced. Wider coverage may improve accuracy, but it does not establish that the resulting account is complete or independent of its viewpoint. The paper assesses an overview by identifying where and when its observations were made, who selected the features recorded, and what remained outside its reach. It distinguishes the extent of coverage from the position of the observer, including the observer's relationship to those supplying information. The mechanism does not require deception or establish that broader views are less reliable. It requires evidence that increased coverage was treated as overcoming limitations that remained. The discussion places the mechanism alongside Donna Haraway's account of situated knowledge and examines three historical and research accounts. In 1790, the Qianlong emperor expanded an investigation of provincial treasury shortages from Shanxi to four provinces. Reported balances led him to dismiss the allegations, although a later emperor stated that officials had transferred holdings to conceal deficits. At the Lushan Conference in 1959, Mao Zedong recalled receiving reports supporting a steel production target he had proposed. His correspondence and Peng Dehuai's account document problems of pressure and inflated reporting without establishing that the number of reports caused Mao's confidence. A contrasting case concerns T. Colin Campbell's participation in a survey of 65 rural Chinese counties, where cholesterol measurements revealed the limits of an earlier comparison with an American average. Part of the Selection and Attention series within On Human Modeling, the paper examines who selects a viewpoint, who determines its coverage, and who can identify what it excludes. Potential applications in human–AI research include aggregated summaries, retrieval systems, and evaluations that distinguish expanded informational coverage from independence of sources, representativeness, or completeness.

items.title: Explain Like I'm Five: Readability of Prostate Cancer Information Can Be Improved by Using Free and Publicly Available Generative Artificial Intelligence Models, Regardless of Prompt
items.abstract: Men with prostate cancer have well‐documented unmet informational needs, yet educational materials often fail to meet recommended readability standards. Freely available generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) chatbots offer a potential solution, though the relative performance of different large language models (LLMs) and prompting strategies remains unclear. This study aims to evaluate the ability of publicly available GenAI chatbots to improve the readability of prostate cancer‐related medical information and determine whether prompt type influences readability outcomes. Eight commonly searched prostate cancer questions were identified through literature review, Google Trends analysis, and ChatGPT‐assisted topic generation. Original responses to these questions were used as source material and submitted to nine freely available GenAI chatbots (ChatGPT 5.2 Instant, DeepSeek V3.2, Grok 4.1 Auto, Qwen3‐Max, Microsoft Copilot Smart, Mistral Le Chat Research, Meta AI [Llama 4], Claude Sonnet 4.5, and Google Gemini 3 Fast). Four readability‐improvement prompts were tested: ‘Explain this in simple terms’, ‘Explain this in plain language’, ‘Explain this like I'm five’, and an engineered prompt designed to maximise readability while preserving content. Responses were analysed using the Flesch‐Kincaid Reading Ease (FKRE) score. Linear mixed‐effects models and estimated marginal means were used to compare prompt, chatbot, and content performance. A total of 285 chatbot responses were analysed. Across all models and prompts, readability improved by a mean of 19.64 points (SD 7.59) compared with baseline. All prompting strategies significantly improved readability (all p ≤ 0.005). The prompt ‘Explain this like I'm five’ produced the greatest improvement, increasing FKRE scores by a mean of 27.70 points (95% CI 15.70–39.69; p < 0.001). All chatbot models significantly improved readability compared with baseline (all p < 0.001). Grok 4.1 Auto achieved the highest overall readability score (mean FKRE 71.81) and greatest mean improvement (+23.33 points), while ChatGPT 5.2 Instant and DeepSeek V3.2 consistently improved readability across all tested prompts and content. Readability improvements varied according to subject matter, with the largest gains observed for bladder function (+29.86 points; p = 0.004) and diagnosis (+27.84 points; p = 0.006). Freely available GenAI chatbots can meaningfully improve the readability of prostate cancer‐related medical information using simple prompts. ‘Explain this like I'm five’ produced the greatest readability gains, though this prompt may reduce clinical nuance and accuracy—an important consideration for medical practitioners. When the most effective lay prompt is uncertain, a curated prompt may offer a reasonable alternative. Further research is required to evaluate the safety, accuracy, and completeness of AI‐simplified prostate cancer content, and to explore how patient eHealth literacy influences engagement with these tools.

items.title: Explainable AI (XAI) for Convolutional Neural Networks in Early Cancer Detection
items.abstract: Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have become useful tools for analysing medical images because they can learn visual patterns associated with normal and abnormal tissue. In cancer screening and diagnosis, however, a high classification score alone is not sufficient: clinicians also need to understand which image regions influenced a model’s output. This paper proposes an explainable deep-learning framework that combines CNN-based image classification with Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) methods to support early cancer detection from histopathological images. The proposed workflow includes image collection, quality assessment, preprocessing, augmentation, CNN training, prediction, and explanation generation. Grad-CAM is used to produce class-specific heatmaps, while LIME and SHAP are considered for local image-region and feature-contribution explanations. The explanations are intended to help users inspect whether the model focuses on tissue regions that are relevant to the predicted class rather than irrelevant background patterns. Model performance can be assessed using accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, specificity, and area under the ROC curve. Explanation quality should additionally be examined through localization agreement, stability, and review by qualified domain experts. The framework is presented as a research proposal; its diagnostic performance and clinical usefulness must be established through controlled experiments and external validation. It is designed as a decision-support approach and is not intended to replace professional diagnosis.

items.title: Explainable AI for Solar PV Power Forecasting: From Model Selection to Trustworthy, Reproducible Deployment
items.abstract: Machine learning (ML) is now a standard tool for forecasting the output of solar photovoltaic (PV) plants, yet published accuracy figures are often hard to compare and harder to trust. Many studies validate with random splits, report no reference forecast, and present feature attributions without saying what they can and cannot show. This paper reviews the main families of ML methods for PV power forecasting and resource assessment, from tree ensembles to deep and foundation models, and sets out a reproducible workflow that combines automated model search with explainable AI. The workflow is then tested on an openly available dataset: a 16.32 kWp plant in Porto, Portugal, forecast one day ahead from a 4 km numerical weather prediction grid. Over a full test year, the best models reach a normalised root mean square error (nRMSE) of 11.6% of installed capacity, about half the error of smart persistence. The choice of input features changed accuracy far more than the choice among strong algorithms, and shuffled cross-validation was mildly optimistic. After conformal calibration, the nominal 80% prediction intervals covered 81.7% of observations, against 64.5% before. SHAP rankings stayed stable when the model was retrained on different periods but shifted when correlated inputs were removed, so attributions should be read as properties of a model rather than of the plant. The paper closes with practical lessons and open problems, including deployment on edge hardware and the effect of a changing climate.

items.title: Explainable AI for Streaming Process Mining: Overview, Challenges and Outlook
items.abstract: Streaming Process Mining (SPM) enables the real-time analysis of business processes through the continuous processing of event streams, providing timely insights and facilitating quick decisions. Although SPM supports various applications in multiple domain areas, it often relies on data-driven algorithms that lack interpretability, limiting user acceptance and trust. To tackle such shortcomings, explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) offers promising techniques to improve transparency and understanding of the applied approach. Despite their complementarity, SPM and XAI originate from distinct research communities, each with its own focus, methodologies, and evaluation criteria. This paper provides an overview of the intersection between XAI and SPM. We categorize existing work according to the SPM tasks addressed, the XAI methodologies used, and the level of interpretability from the end-user’s perspective. In addition, we identify key research challenges and propose future directions aimed at developing more human-centered and trustworthy SPM approaches. Our findings emphasize the importance of aligning algorithmic performance and human comprehension to support responsible decision making in dynamic process environments.

items.title: Explainable artificial intelligence for prehospital identification of endovascular thrombectomy candidates: a retrospective real-world study
items.abstract: Acute ischaemic stroke due to large-vessel occlusion requires rapid endovascular treatment (EVT). Prehospital stroke scales, though widely used, have not achieved an optimal balance of sensitivity, specificity, and overall discriminative performance, underlining the need for evaluation of machine learning (ML) approaches to improve early identification of EVT candidates. We conducted a retrospective development and internal validation study based on digital real-world data from consecutive EMS-transported patients with suspected stroke ( n = 1,435, 94 EVT events [6.6%]) from the Stroke Angel initiative in a rural region in Germany (Rhön-Grabfeld), covering the period from January 2015 to June 2021. Predicted probabilities of six ML models were recalibrated using Platt scaling, and clinical relevance was evaluated using decision curve analysis (DCA). SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) values were computed to quantify individual feature contributions to model predictions. Among 287 patients (24 EVT events) in the evaluation cohort, Random Forest achieved the highest AUROC (0.85 [95% CI, 0.78–0.90]), with sensitivity of 0.92 [0.74–0.99], specificity of 0.66 [0.60–0.72]. The 4I-SS (score > 2) yielded an AUROC of 0.82 [0.72–0.89], sensitivity of 0.87 [0.67–0.96], and specificity of 0.69 [0.64–0.74]. Bootstrapped intervals overlapped across all metrics and platt scaling probabilities, suggesting no statistically significant superiority.

items.title: Explainable Machine Learning for Classifying Documented Death Outcomes in FDA Adverse-Event Reports: A Multi-Quarter Exploratory Study and Pharmacovigilance Framework
items.abstract: Objective To describe an explainable artificial intelligence pharmacovigilance framework and evaluate whether machine-learning models can classify FDA spontaneous adverse-event reports that document a death outcome, while clearly distinguishing retrospective report classification from prospective patient-level prediction. Methods We analyzed official FDA AEMS/FAERS ASCII quarterly extracts from 2020 Q1 through 2025 Q1 (21 quarters). Reports without a recorded outcome-table entry were excluded. A report was labelled positive when at least one OUTC row recorded the DE (death) code; other reports with recorded outcomes formed the comparison class. We excluded case identifiers listed in the supplied quarterly deletion files and retained one report version per CASEID using the highest CASEVERSION, then FDA receipt date and PRIMARYID as tie-breakers. A disk-backed SQLite workflow resolved versions across quarters. A bounded sample was drawn within chronological fit (2020–June 2023), calibration (July–December 2023), and test (2024 Q1–2025 Q1) windows. Logistic regression and histogram-based gradient boosting were fitted, sigmoid-calibrated on the separate calibration sample, and assessed on the held-out test sample. The operating threshold for each model was selected by maximizing F1 on the calibration sample. Subgroup metrics and TreeSHAP explanations were evaluated on sampled test records. Results After outcome filtering, deletion-list exclusion, case-version resolution and removal of records without usable FDA receipt dates, the analysis cohort contained 4,534,679 report versions/cases, including 667,062 reports with a recorded DE outcome and 3,867,617 reports with other recorded outcomes. The model sample included 250,000 fit reports, 75,000 calibration reports and 150,000 chronological test reports. In the test sample, gradient boosting achieved ROC-AUC 0.722 and average precision 0.343, compared with 0.657 and 0.247 for logistic regression. At thresholds selected on the calibration sample to maximize F1, gradient boosting achieved death-class precision 0.304, recall 0.469, F1 0.369 and balanced accuracy 0.645; its Brier score was 0.110. SHAP summaries ranked reaction-row count, age, sex, reporter type, occupation code and country-related fields among the leading model features. These are report-level associations and may reflect reporting and documentation processes. Conclusion The multi-quarter analysis demonstrates that a carefully defined retrospective report-classification task can be evaluated reproducibly across FDA quarterly extracts. items.title: Exploring EFL students’ critical AI literacy in generative AI-assisted essay revision: insights into profiles and trajectories
items.abstract: This study examines how English as a foreign language (EFL) students demonstrate and develop Critical AI Literacy (CAIL) in generative AI-assisted essay revision. Drawing on the APSE model, which conceptualizes CAIL across four dimensions (awareness, positionality, interaction strategies, and evaluation), we conducted a longitudinal case study of three focal students across four writing tasks throughout a semester. Data sources included student-AI interaction logs, think-aloud protocols, stimulated recall interviews, and both initial and revised essay drafts. Qualitative analyses were conducted to trace patterns and changes in students’ CAIL. Findings show that all three students demonstrated CAIL across the four dimensions, although critical evaluation and critical positionality emerged as the most salient dimensions. Students selectively integrated AI feedback based on rhetorical fit, linguistic appropriateness, and factual accuracy, demonstrating various levels of agency. Over time, two students became increasingly selective and context-sensitive in their engagement with AI, whereas the third demonstrated strategic engagement from the outset but showed substantial task-to-task variation in feedback uptake. Overall, the students’ trajectories were heterogeneous and task-dependent rather than uniformly progressive. These patterns challenge linear models of AI literacy and highlight its situated nature in EFL writing contexts. Pedagogically, the study calls for differentiated instruction that fosters evaluative judgment and self-representation alongside prompt design. The findings contribute to a growing body of research advocating for more nuanced, learner-centered approaches to AI integration in foreign language writing.

items.title: Extending qualified research institutions beyond the investigational new drug application
items.abstract: To renew US competitiveness in clinical trials, the federal government launched Operation TrialBlazer in June 2026. Its proposed Expedited-IND Acceleration Pilot would enlist Qualified Research Institutions (QRIs) to help sponsors prepare investigational new drug (IND) applications for first-in-human studies. Because a successful IND does not guarantee a completed trial, we propose a testable, expanded QRI framework to support trial execution. First, build QRIs with standing networks that reuse contracts, data systems, and staff to lower marginal costs and enable performance measurement. Second, require QRIs to have capabilities that enable and assess site performance: human factors expertise and stakeholder co-design in protocol development; leading (not only lagging) indicators of trial performance; efficient, proportionate execution that preserves rigor and safety; and oversight by an independent trial performance monitoring board empowered to conduct in-person observations and interviews at trial sites. Third, qualify QRIs on demonstrated performance, with reciprocal obligations for sponsors. Fourth, renew QRIs using publicly reported, case-mix-adjusted metrics. The Food and Drug Administration and National Institutes of Health should jointly fund evaluations of this framework. Extending QRIs across the trial lifecycle is more likely than a pre-IND role alone to close the time and cost gaps that send research overseas.

items.title: Eye and Face Protection Violations Have Ranked Among OSHA’s Top 10 Since 2018: An Evidence-Based Framework for Intelligent Detection, Risk Assessment, and Timely Intervention
items.abstract: Eye and face protection violations under the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) standard have repeatedly appeared among the most frequently cited federal workplace safety standards since fiscal year 2018, highlighting persistent challenges in personal protective equipment (PPE) compliance, hazard recognition, and occupational safety management. Workers in construction, manufacturing, and other high-risk industrial environments remain vulnerable to eye and facial injuries arising from flying particles, chemical splashes, molten materials, dust, and other hazardous exposures. Although conventional workplace inspections, safety training, and supervisory monitoring remain essential, these approaches are often constrained by limited observation coverage, intermittent assessments, delayed identification of violations, and inconsistent enforcement. Advances in artificial intelligence (AI), computer vision, and edge computing offer opportunities to strengthen PPE monitoring through automated recognition, contextual risk assessment, and timely corrective intervention. This study examines the regulatory, technological, and operational challenges associated with persistent eye and face protection violations and develops an evidence-based framework for integrating AI-assisted PPE detection with proactive occupational safety management. Specifically, it investigates how deep learning-based object detection, worker–PPE association, pose estimation, edge inference, hazard-aware decision rules, and human-centered intervention mechanisms can improve the identification, prioritization, and resolution of potentially unsafe PPE practices. An evidence-based narrative synthesis was conducted using OSHA regulatory information and peer-reviewed literature addressing occupational eye and face injuries, PPE compliance monitoring, computer vision architectures, machine learning, workplace hazard assessment, and safety management systems. Particular attention was given to You Only Look Once (YOLO)-based detection models, pose and key point estimation, lightweight edge-computing architectures, temporal tracking, and multiclass PPE classification. Existing studies were critically examined to identify methodological strengths, operational limitations, performance variability, and research gaps. Building on the reviewed evidence, this study develops a risk-informed occupational eye and face protection assessment methodology that integrates regulatory requirements, hazard exposure, protective equipment adequacy, monitoring reliability, and corrective intervention effectiveness. Rather than proposing another automated PPE detection architecture, the methodology examines how technology-generated observations can be interpreted within task-specific safety requirements and translated into measurable intervention priorities. It distinguishes confirmed equipment absence, incorrect positioning, unsuitable protection, and insufficient visual evidence while incorporating mathematical indicators for hazard-weighted prioritization, detection reliability, corrective-action timeliness, and occupational injury incidence. Computer vision and edge-based monitoring are examined as supporting sources of safety evidence rather than independent injury-prevention solutions. The resulting methodology provides a structured basis for prospective evaluation of monitoring-supported safety interventions. No newly trained detection model, experimental dataset, or completed field trial is reported. Unlike conventional PPE recognition systems that primarily identify equipment presence, the framework emphasizes whether appropriate protective equipment is correctly positioned, associated with the exposed worker, and suitable for the prevailing occupational hazard. It also incorporates human oversight, privacy safeguards, explainable decision support, and mechanisms for managing false-positive detections and ambiguous visual conditions. The study proposes a multidimensional evaluation strategy extending beyond conventional computer vision metrics such as precision, recall, mean average precision, and inference speed. Recommended performance indicators include event-level violation detection sensitivity, false alerts per worker-hour, end-to-end notification latency, time to verified corrective action, unresolved hazardous exposure duration, recurrence of PPE violations, and longitudinal occupational injury outcomes. The proposed framework provides a structured basis for comparing AI-assisted monitoring with conventional safety inspection approaches while distinguishing technical detection performance from operational intervention effectiveness. It further identifies research priorities involving small-object recognition, transparent protective eyewear detection, cross-site generalizability, risk-based alert optimization, worker privacy, and prospective validation of injury-prevention outcomes. AI-assisted eye and face protection monitoring represents a promising approach to addressing persistent PPE compliance challenges through continuous observation, contextual violation assessment, and timely intervention. However, high detection accuracy and rapid alert generation alone do not demonstrate reductions in occupational injuries. Effective prevention requires reliable worker - PPE association, hazard-specific compliance assessment, accountable human intervention, verified corrective action, and integration with established occupational safety procedures. The proposed framework advances the conceptual foundation for transforming automated PPE recognition into a measurable, human-centered workplace safety intervention. Future empirical research should validate the framework across diverse industrial environments and determine whether improved violation detection and corrective-action timeliness translate into sustained reductions in hazardous exposure and preventable eye and face injuries.

items.title: Feasibility of a Chatbot-Based Intervention to Support Case Management for Patients at Risk of Suicide in the Emergency Department: A Pilot Study
items.abstract: Background/Objectives: Emergency departments (EDs) are critical for suicide prevention, yet high workloads often hinder consistent case management. This pilot study assessed the clinical feasibility, usability, and acceptability of CAREBot, a rule-based chatbot designed to support ED-based case management for patients at risk of suicide, among patients and social workers. Methods: We employed an explanatory sequential mixed-methods design. Ten patients and three social workers used CAREBot and completed questionnaires assessing usability, perceived usefulness, and satisfaction. Patients’ psychological status was repeatedly assessed using the PHQ-9, GAD-7, and SBQ-R. Semi-structured interviews with social workers explored integration challenges and workflow impacts. Results: Patients rated ease of use (3.9/5) and information clarity (4.4/5) favorably, whereas emotional comfort was rated lower (2.5/5). Over 4 weeks, 191 URL access events were recorded among the 10 patients (mean, 19.1 per patient). Individual PHQ-9, GAD-7, and SBQ-R score trajectories varied across participants, with both increases and decreases observed. Social workers rated CAREBot favorably for quickly understanding patients’ risk level or condition (4.33/5) and ease of following the scenario flow (5.0/5). Qualitative findings suggested that CAREBot could support initial patient assessments through structured digital screening, although social workers raised concerns regarding risk-scoring accuracy and the management of multiple high-risk patients. Conclusions: CAREBot appears to be feasible and acceptable as an adjunct to ED-based suicide case management, although these preliminary findings require confirmation in larger controlled studies. A rule-based architecture was deliberately selected to provide predictable and controlled interactions in a high-risk environment. Future research should evaluate whether integrating large language models (LLMs) with rule-based safety mechanisms can improve conversational responsiveness and personalization while maintaining patient safety.

items.title: Female anatomies disguise ECG abnormalities following myocardial infarction: An artificial intelligence−enabled modelling and simulation study
items.abstract: The ECG is modulated by torso-heart anatomy, challenging patients' diagnosis and risk stratification. This study aims to quantify how torso-heart anatomical factors affect sex differences in ECG biomarkers in acute and chronic myocardial infarction (MI). We exploit the perfect control of artificial intelligence (AI)-augmented multiscale modelling and simulation, using clinical magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and ECGs for model construction and validation. A cohort of 1720 torso-ventricular anatomies (50% female) was constructed from MRIs of healthy and post-MI participants in the UK Biobank. A total of 8600 simulations were performed considering anatomical variability, three electrophysiological stages (healthy, ischaemic and infarcted) and two infarct locations (anteroseptal and inferolateral). Quantifying the effect of cardiac size, position and orientation on each ECG biomarker, we found that female anatomies had larger distances between infarct and ECG electrodes (relative to cardiac size) and larger angles between infarct normal and ECG lead axes, both primarily caused by their more superior cardiac position. This reduced ST elevation and amplitude of late depolarisation and repolarisation tails, ultimately shortening QRS duration (QRSd) and T-peak-to-end interval (TpTe). Overall, position and orientation of the heart impacted TpTe more severely than QRSd; our AI-enabled mechanistic modelling and simulation identified smaller ventricles, superior cardiac position and different ventricular orientation as key anatomical contributors of QRSd, TpTe and ST elevation being reduced in female versus male anatomies. Our framework provides a blueprint for quantifying the impact of anatomical sex differences on functional markers and enables future work in tailoring clinical guidelines considering unique patient anatomy to reduce biased outcomes. KEY POINTS: The ECG, important in diagnosing and managing treatment for myocardial infarction (heart attacks), is known to be impacted by the anatomy of the heart and torso. Women suffering myocardial infarction are underdiagnosed, and the effect of anatomical sex differences on the ECG in myocardial infarction is poorly understood. Our human computational modelling and simulation demonstrate that ST elevation in ischaemia was reduced in female anatomies, mainly as their hearts are higher in the torso than male anatomies. We show that ECG time intervals were affected differently by anatomy: the T-peak-to-end interval was more sensitive to cardiac positioning, whereas QRS duration was more sensitive to cardiac size. Our study demonstrates how computer simulations provide an efficient mechanistic tool to quantify the role of anatomical differences in clinical biomarkers and could ultimately support the inclusion of sex differences in clinical guidelines.

items.title: Financial–Structural Conditions and Perceived Low-Carbon Performance in Hotels: Organizational and Technological Pathways from a Sociotechnical Perspective
items.abstract: The transition toward a low-carbon hotel sector involves more than the availability of financing or the adoption of technology. It also relates to the ability to transform available resources into usable technical capabilities and organizational commitments that can sustain the implementation of environmental initiatives. Drawing on the sociotechnical systems (STS) perspective, this study examines how financial–structural enabling conditions (FSECs) relate to perceived low-carbon performance (PLCP) through two parallel mechanisms: organizational ethical commitment to sustainability (OESC) and green technological capability (GTC). Using a sample of 587 informants—67 managers and 520 employees—from 103 hotels in Extremadura, Spain, the proposed relationships are analyzed through partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). The results show that more favorable FSECs have a positive direct relationship with perceived low-carbon performance and are also associated with greater development of GTC and OESC. Both mechanisms are positively related to performance, and both proposed indirect pathways receive empirical support. Theoretically, this study extends the sociotechnical perspective on hotel sustainability by positioning FSECs as an enabling context related to environmental performance through distinct but simultaneous organizational and technological mechanisms. Practically, it provides guidance for environmental investment and the design of support programs tailored to hotels’ conditions and needs.

items.title: Fine-tuning and retrieval augmentation for crystallography and cryo-EM question answering using a community-derived corpus
items.abstract: Structural biology mailing lists such as CCP4, CCP-EM, Phenix and COOT contain decades of expert answers to practical problems, but an answer is difficult to find even when it has been given before. A question-and-answer corpus was built from 103,600 messages across the four mailing lists, and threads were classified as questions. The answers were confirmed by the asker’s reply or by the agreement of several participants, identified by three LLM models. items.title: Fire the Neuron: An Interactive Learning Tool for Exploring Neuronal Signaling
items.abstract: Fire the Neuron is an interactive learning tool designed to reinforce foundational concepts in neuronal physiology through active engagement with immediate feedback. The activity guides students through nine progressive stages exploring the electrical and chemical events involved in neuronal communication. Throughout the activity, students investigate graded potentials, action potential generation, depolarization, repolarization, hyperpolarization, refractory periods, action potential propagation, and synaptic transmission. Interactive components challenge students to calculate changes in membrane potential, predict whether threshold will be reached, identify the roles of voltage-gated ion channels, and examine the effects of myelination and demyelination on signal propagation. Students also sequence events involved in synaptic transmission and investigate disruptions in neuronal communication. Immediate feedback provides opportunities to evaluate responses, identify misconceptions, and reinforce understanding. The tool is designed primarily for undergraduate anatomy and physiology courses but may also be appropriate for introductory neuroscience and related courses. Instructors can incorporate it into classroom activities, assign it as an independent learning exercise, or recommend it as a supplemental resource for reviewing course material and preparing for examinations. Fire the Neuron is freely accessible through GitHub Pages and can be completed using a standard web browser without downloading additional software or creating an account. The tool was developed with the assistance of generative artificial intelligence (AI), with the instructional content, scientific accuracy, and pedagogical design guided and reviewed by the author. items.title: Flexible Data Access Mechanisms for IoT Ecosystems: From Content-Based Addressing to LLM-Driven Data Acquisition
items.abstract: The continuous development and integration of public and private Internet of Things (IoT) infrastructures require flexible and scalable data access mechanisms that ensure seamless access to IoT data regardless of its source of physical address. Traditionally, retrieving data from different physical sources requires rigid, topology-dependent protocols and high technical skills; this may limit accessibility for a wider range of end-users.Content-Based Addressing (CBA) accesses data based on its attributes or content rather than its network location. Users need an intuitive mechanism to extract IoT values from multiple sources (e.g. public and private sources), removing the need for technical database query knowledge. In a similar way to web search (e.g. Google), users ask questions in natural language based on content, location and time without direct reference to the physical location of the IoT devices that provide the necessary information. This paper proposes a novel, hybrid framework for flexible IoT data access that combines CBA with a Large Language Model (LLM)-based conversational interface. The architecture is built on two core pillars: a Content-Addressable Storage (CAS) layer, coupled with a device registry, that unifies heterogeneous data sources, public APIs and private edge devices, into a single content-addressed store secured by a granular Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) mechanism. The second pillar is a Natural Language Query Engine that translates chat-based interrogations into executable system queries.An adaptive imputation service maintains data completeness by detecting missing sensor readings, predicting replacement values, and reconciling predictions when delayed measurements arrive. Together, the framework enables an intuitive experience for IoT data exploration with no technical training needed.

items.title: Flexible Mo 2 TiC 2 T x /TaS 2 van der Waals heterostructure films for bias-free dual-mode sensing and EMI shielding
items.abstract: Developing flexible electronics that integrate multimodal sensing, bias-free signal generation, and electromagnetic interference (EMI) shielding is critical for wearable health monitoring, artificial intelligence, and human–computer interaction. Semiconducting Mo2TiC2Tx MXene films show promise for flexible thermoelectrics and EMI shielding, but their relatively low electrical conductivity restricts both the power factor (PF) and the overall EMI shielding effectiveness (SE). Here, we report a van der Waals heterostructure film of Mo2TiC2Tx/TaS2 fabricated via intercalation–exfoliation followed by vacuum-assisted filtration. Heterointerface engineering simultaneously enhances thermoelectric performance and EMI shielding. The electrical conductivity reaches 878.3 S·cm−1 (~23-fold enhancement), and the PF reaches 14.4 μW·m−1·K−2 (~4-fold), while the EMI SE improves from 14.1 to 40.6 dB. The film enables dual-mode sensing free from crosstalk, temperature detection via the Seebeck effect and pressure sensing via piezoresistive response, while maintaining stable signal fidelity under external EMI. Furthermore, the film exhibits photothermoelectric and Joule-heating responses. Integrated with a wireless acquisition module for signal readout and transmission, the sensor enables real-time transmission of temperature and pressure signals. This work provides a strategy for designing flexible heterostructures that synergistically combine bias-free signal generation, multimodal sensing, EMI resilience, and multistimulus responsiveness for next-generation smart electronics.

items.title: FLUID: Flexible, Evidence-Grounded Situated Task Guidance
items.abstract: Real-time task guidance is inherently flexible: when an agent guides a user through a task, multiple responses and timings can be appropriate, and sometimes the best action is to remain silent. Existing benchmarks often miss this flexibility by treating synthesized dialogues as fixed targets for what to say and when to say it. We introduce FLUID (Flexible, Evidence-Grounded Situated Task Guidance), a unified framework for modeling, evaluating, and enabling flexible interaction in multimodal task guidance. Using naturally occurring human-human guidance from WTaG and HoloAssist, FLUID grounds interventions in their supporting evidence, necessity, and timing flexibility, and uses this representation both to evaluate flexible guidance and to build a real-time agent for task guidance. Our agent achieves the strongest overall balance of response correctness, intervention precision, timely guidance, and response latency among evaluated systems, while still leaving room for improvement in avoiding speech overlap. Together, FLUID moves situated task guidance beyond rigid reference matching toward more natural and adaptive human-AI interaction. Project page: https://fluid-guidance.github.io.

items.title: FoMo-X: Modular Explainability Signals for Outlier Detection Foundation Models
items.abstract: Tabular foundation models, specifically Prior-Data Fitted Networks (PFNs), have revolutionized outlier detection (OD) by enabling unsupervised zero-shot adaptation to new datasets without training. However, despite their predictive power, these models typically function as opaque black boxes, outputting scalar outlier scores that lack the operational context required for safety-critical decision-making. Existing post-hoc explanation methods are often computationally prohibitive for real-time deployment or fail to capture the epistemic uncertainty inherent in zero-shot inference. In this work, we introduce FoMo-X, a modular framework that equips OD foundation models with intrinsic, lightweight diagnostic capabilities. We leverage the insight that the frozen embeddings of a pretrained PFN backbone already encode rich, context-conditioned relational information. FoMo-X attaches auxiliary diagnostic heads to these embeddings, trained offline using the same generative simulator prior as the backbone. This allows us to distill computationally expensive properties, such as Monte Carlo dropout based epistemic uncertainty, into a deterministic, single-pass inference. We instantiate FoMo-X with two novel heads: a Severity Head that discretizes deviations into interpretable risk tiers, and an Uncertainty Head that provides calibrated confidence measures. Extensive evaluation on synthetic and real-world benchmarks (ADBench) demonstrates that FoMo-X recovers ground-truth diagnostic signals with high fidelity and negligible inference overhead. By bridging the gap between foundation model performance and operational explainability, FoMo-X offers a scalable path toward trustworthy, zero-shot outlier detection.

items.title: FoodReact-AR: Learning Audience Reactions that Zero-Shot LLMs Miss in Arabic Food-Insecurity Discourse
items.abstract: Facebook reactions record how an audience received a post, a signal absent from the post's text. We treat the six differentiated reactions on 74,241 Arabic food-insecurity posts from public Facebook pages (2020-2024) as compositions, apply a centered log-ratio transformation, and cluster them into four audience profiles: Solidarity (Love-dominant), Dismissal (Haha-dominant), Grief (Sad-dominant), and a flat Ambivalent profile. Dismissal peaks in 2022 (22.3%), the year of the wheat price shock, and grief in 2024 (14.0%), during the Gaza food emergency; a page-clustered GEE confirms both shifts (odds ratios 2.18 and 1.34), and they survive minimum-reaction filtering, alternative zero replacements and clustering methods, and bootstrap resampling. We then test whether the profiles can be predicted without reactions. A zero-shot Arabic LLM recovers Grief for 83.8% of posts but Dismissal for only 3.4%, and in a matched ablation, it shows the reaction percentages do not help. A simple classifier trained on the reaction-derived labels and tested on unseen pages recovers dismissal for 60.0% (macro-F1 0.56 against 0.43), mainly from mentions of officials and institutions. Derisive audience responses are thus learnable from text, yet a zero-shot LLM misses them. We release the corpus, LLM, and human annotation layers, and an evaluation protocol as FoodReact-AR.

items.title: FRAMING OF THE US-CHINA AI RACE IN PAKISTANI AND WESTERN MEDIA: IMPLICATIONS FOR GLOBAL POWER POLITICS. A QUANTITATIVE MAPPING OF EXISTING RESEARCH
items.abstract: The competition between the United States and China for artificial intelligence (AI) is often presented as a race, and news media is one place where this race narrative is being created. However, there is little empirical research that looks at this framing, and of that little research, where did it come from - and what voices were left out? The article provides a quantitative mapping of 14 empirical studies of news coverage of AI and of US-China technology rivalry, which were identified by a series of structured web-based searches in November 2026. All studies were coded for sample context, method, scale of data, year of publication, thematic focus and main findings, and the frequencies, proportions and Wilson 95% confidence intervals are reported. It is important to note that the mapping revealed that there were eight studies (64.3%) that focused on US and Chinese media, two (14.3%) that included a South Asian sample, and none of the 14 studies discussed Pakistani media coverage on the US-China AI race. With reference to the concept of framing and the notion of sociotechnical imaginaries, the patterns are explained, five propositions that can be tested in relation to framing the race in Pakistan and the West are offered, and a research agenda for comparative analysis is recommended. The study does not make new claims about media content itself, but an evidence-based account of a research gap. Keywords: Framing; artificial intelligence; US-China rivalry; soft power; Pakistan; media research; scoping review; global communication

items.title: From AI Dialogue to Open Access: Making a Scholar's Foundational Works Accessible
items.abstract: This reflective case study documents how sustained collaboration with ChatGPT helped Jean-Pol Martin make his doctoral dissertation (1985) and habilitation thesis (1994) openly accessible. According to Martin’s retrospective account, AI dialogue introduced publication possibilities he had not previously considered and supported the organization of a process involving digitization, publisher permission, legal assistance and coordination with the University Library of Eichstätt-Ingolstadt. Over approximately two months, at a reported cost of EUR 400, both foundational works were made available through Zenodo and the university’s publication server, KU.edoc. The dissertation’s two microfiche supplements were also digitized and published. Inclusion of the digital editions in the library catalogue was pending at the reporting cut-off. The paper examines the complementary contributions of AI assistance, human initiative and institutional infrastructure. Its contribution to the ongoing exploration of Martin’s human-AI model is a documented implementation process whose outputs extend beyond jointly generated text: publicly accessible primary sources. The study distinguishes demonstrated accessibility from potential future effects on discovery, scholarly reception and citation impact. It also addresses limitations concerning retrospective testimony, machine readability and long-term preservation. Prepared with ChatGPT assistance; presented as a reflective working paper, not as peer-reviewed research.

items.title: From Blisters on Vipers to Nanobubbles in Vessels: A Review of Biological Decompression Bubbles
items.abstract: Decompression sickness (DCS) is an occupational health problem fundamentally driven by the formation of gas bubbles in the human body, which could be a threat to the life of divers, astronauts and hyperbaric workers. The phenomenon of bubble formation in organisms after decompression provided the earliest experimental evidence for decompression theory. Since then, researchers across different eras have conducted extensive work on biological decompression bubbles, which brought about the establishment of gas nuclei theory. While Yount’s quantitatively calculable Varying Permeability Model (VPM) has been successfully applied to decompression algorithms, its core assumption—the “surface-active skin”—remains experimentally unverified. But recent developments in research on nanobubbles and the Active Hydrophobic Spots (AHS) hypothesis have provided new physicochemical perspectives. This review critically evaluates the theoretical evolution and experimental progress in this field, integrating recent advances in molecular dynamics and interfacial physics. To contribute to shedding light on the unresolved paradox of biological decompression bubbles in vivo, we highlight the significance of the paradigm shift from macroscopic gas dissolution to interfacial mechanics, which may help identify the missing links in current DCS research and outline a new multidisciplinary path forward.

items.title: From Cases to Criteria: Reusing Evaluation Knowledge for Task-Specific Rubric Generation
items.abstract: Query-specific rubrics make LLM evaluation more fine-grained and transparent, and generating high-quality rubrics requires both identifying the target query's evaluation scope and specifying concrete checks. Historical rubrics provide reusable evaluation experiences, yet existing approaches reuse either complete query-rubric cases or aggregated criteria and dimensions without explicitly connecting recurring evaluation requirements to their criterion-level evidence and source-query context. This can preserve irrelevant task details or lose the broader evaluation structure. In this paper, we introduce RubricDuo, which organizes historical query-rubric pairs into a Rubric Knowledge Graph linking evaluation dimensions, shared concepts, local concepts, criteria, and queries, where reusable evaluation requirements across queries are abstracted by shared concepts. Given a target query, RubricDuo first combines concepts relevant to the target query with retrieved historical cases to draft a rubric with broad coverage. It then revisits each draft criterion, retrieves concept-linked historical criteria and their source queries, and adapts applicable evidence to refine the criterion. Experiments on RubricBench and HealthBench demonstrate that RubricDuo achieves the overall best performance among the evaluated automatic methods in both alignment with human-authored rubrics and downstream LLM judging.

items.title: From Data Alignment to Parameter Generation: Few-Shot Cross-City Traffic Prediction with Conditional Diffusion
items.abstract: Accurate mobile traffic forecasting is crucial for network service management, supporting proactive capacity provisioning, congestion mitigation, and energy-efficient operation. However, many cities and regions are data-scarce (e.g., newly deployed or poorly instrumented areas), thus making traffic prediction a few-shot learning problem and limiting the practicality of standard data-driven models. Existing cross-city solutions primarily rely on data-space alignment to match traffic distributions between data-rich and data-scarce cities, but such alignment is often brittle under real-world distribution shifts, measurement noise, and city-specific bias. To address these limitations, we propose a Conditional Diffusion-based Parameter Generation (CDPG) framework. Instead of aligning raw data, CDPG learns the conditional distribution of high-performing predictor parameters for source cities and directly generates node-specific model parameters for the target city. To support reliable adaptation for network traffic prediction, CDPG conditions parameter generation on multi-modal spatio-temporal context. Specifically, CDPG captures spatial environment cues by combining satellite imagery with large language model (LLM)-derived semantic descriptions, and summarizes complex temporal behaviors via unsupervised pattern clustering. These contextual components guide CDPG in producing parameters tailored to each base station's operational context, thereby improving robustness under cross-city and cross-region shifts. Extensive experiments on three large-scale datasets show that CDPG consistently outperforms state-of-the-art cross-city few-shot baselines by up to 9.72% on standard forecasting metrics and remains robust for few-shot multi-step prediction. The code is available at https://github.com/LingoodBoy/CDPG.

items.title: From data scarcity to data abundance: big data, artificial intelligence and the transformation of knowledge production in the social sciences
items.abstract: The article examines the development of data-driven research in contemporary social sciences amid the growing use of big data, machine learning, and artificial intelligence. The aim of the study is to analyze publication trends, the thematic structure of this research field, and the prevalence of critical discourse concerning the methodological and epistemological limitations of digital technologies. The empirical dataset comprises 3,779 English-language scientific articles published between 1995 and 2025 and indexed in the Scopus database. The study employs bibliometric analysis, natural language processing (NLP), latent Dirichlet allocation (LDA) topic modeling, bigram analysis, and dictionary-based identification of critical themes. Particular attention is given to data quality, measurement validity, algorithmic bias, and risks associated with generative artificial intelligence. The findings demonstrate substantial growth in publication activity since the 2010s and a shift in thematic emphasis from big data toward machine learning and artificial intelligence. Topic modeling reveals considerable thematic heterogeneity despite the application of similar analytical approaches. Indicators of critical discourse are identified across different thematic areas, although their prevalence remains limited: relevant publications accounted for 9.2% of the annual dataset in 2024 and 9.0% in 2025. The findings indicate that quantitative research expansion is accompanied by thematic fragmentation and a relatively small proportion of publications containing identifiable indicators of critical reflection. The scientific significance of the study lies in systematizing research trends and thematic structures, while its practical significance concerns improving social research methodology and teaching data analysis methods. However, term-frequency analysis cannot directly assess the depth of critical reflection or the degree of theoretical integration within the social sciences. This limitation should be considered when interpreting the findings and drawing broader conclusions. Keywords: big data, artificial intelligence, datafication, machine learning, critical reflection, digitalization.

items.title: From Data to Verified Model Knowledge: How Evidence Access Shapes Large Language Model Answers About Trained Machine-Learning Classifiers
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to answer questions about predictive models, but a fluent answer about a model is not necessarily true of it. We propose a framework in which every answer is checked against a reference that independent software computes from the fitted model. The main finding is simple: the LLM was much more accurate when software had done the calculations than when it had to work them out from the model itself. In a confirmatory study with Gemini 2.5 Flash, the LLM correctly answered 16 of 36 questions whose answer follows exactly from the full model description, such as a prediction or a decision path, but 33 of the same 36 once software had computed the values from which the answer follows. A replication with 50 classifiers, five datasets and three LLM configurations, including a reasoning setting and an open-weight model, reproduced this pattern. Without model information, the LLMs declined to answer or guessed at chance level, and verified answers were reported faithfully once their origin was stated. Model-specific calculations should therefore be left to verified software, while the LLM reports and explains the checked results.

items.title: From field-scale to large-scale spectral libraries: Tabular foundation models in soil spectroscopy
items.abstract: Visible and near-infrared (vis–NIR) and mid-infrared (MIR) spectroscopy enable rapid, cost-effective prediction of soil properties. Yet, translating high-dimensional, highly collinear spectra into accurate soil property predictions remains challenging, particularly when employing machine learning. We systematically investigated regression models and dimensionality reduction approaches for spectroscopic modeling across 85 soil property prediction tasks from open benchmark datasets in pedometrics, spanning field-scale digital soil mapping and a global soil spectral library. We compared an in-context learning tabular foundation model (TabPFN), a convolutional neural network (CNN), rule-based regression (Cubist), Random Forest, and partial least squares regression (PLSR) using full spectra as well as features derived from principal component analysis (PCA) and partial least squares (PLS) latent variables. TabPFN consistently delivered the best overall performance across spectral regions, properties, and scales, including large spectral library tasks with tens of thousands of soil samples. Notably, TabPFN applied directly to full spectra already surpassed all classical baselines, showing that explicit dimensionality reduction is not strictly required for strong performance. Further improvements were achieved through PLS, which proved to be an effective dimensionality reduction strategy for all models. Combining PLS latent variables with TabPFN yielded the best predictions overall, lowering the root mean squared error (RMSE) relative to the strongest classical baseline on 44 of the 46 large-scale spectral library tasks, by a median of 14%. Our findings provide evidence-based guidance for spectroscopic calibration model selection across operational scales, demonstrating that the long-standing advantages of PLSR and modern tabular foundation models complement each other in chemometrics.

items.title: From Fields Medalists' Concerns to Hidden Capture: A Tale of Two Simulated Worlds of Human Cognition
items.abstract: Hidden capture is a loss of skill that the people losing it do not notice, combined with a dependence that does not reverse when the pressure behind it eases. The Correction Freeze Problem predicts this pattern, but testing it on human thinking would take decades of data that do not yet exist for generative AI. We therefore built a computer simulation of a population, calibrated to what can be measured today, and followed it across generations in two worlds that share the same machines. In World M, AI mostly replaces people’s own practice, and each generation learns what normal ability looks like from the one before. In World N, AI mostly supports practice, and each generation’s sense of normal ability is anchored in direct experience, including time in nature. The model reproduces today’s rise of AI-written text in student work, the share of people who check AI output, and how loosely people’s opinions of their own thinking track tested performance. The simulations show what a captured world would be like from the inside. Delegation stays modest for a while and then sweeps through most of the population within a few years, because each person who hands over their thinking makes it more normal for everyone else. Skill then drains away without being felt. In World M, the average person’s unaided ability fell to about the bottom tenth of the population before AI, yet people registered only a small part of that loss, about a quarter even a century later, because their machine-assisted work looked as good as ever and everyone around them had declined too. The habit of checking disappeared first: at full delegation, only two people in a hundred still compared the machine’s answers with their own judgment, and when the machine’s error rate was quietly doubled, about one in a hundred noticed within five years. In an illustrative century, easing the pressure after a generation of heavy delegation restored only World N; the other two worlds were still captured half a century later. Staying out of the trap proved far easier than climbing out of it. These findings are conditional projections, not forecasts. Across 2,176 sensitivity runs, the unseen loss appeared every time, and its size depended mainly on two things societies can influence now: whether AI replaces or supports people’s own practice, and whether each generation anchors its sense of competence in direct experience. Whether capture can be undone depended on one quantity not yet measured, how much an individual’s reliance on AI changes from year to year; if reliance churns, capture becomes reversible, though it stays hidden. Several earlier results weakened as the model was corrected, and the main pre-specified test of a final extension came back negative; both are reported.

items.title: From materials to meaning: Teachers’ interpretative labour and the joy of planning in discretionary spaces
items.abstract: Curriculum planning takes time and energy. As concerns about teacher workload and workforce shortages intensify, many education systems are turning to scripted curriculum materials and emerging generative artificial intelligence (GAI) tools to support planning, assuming that reducing curriculum work will alleviate teachers’ widely recognised time poverty. Such responses position curriculum planning as a task to be streamlined, standardised, or outsourced. However, they risk oversimplifying the complexity of curriculum work and undervaluing the interpretative processes teachers engage in to meet the diverse needs of their students. Drawing on interviews with eight teachers and curriculum leaders in Australian Capital Territory (ACT) public primary schools, this paper examines how teachers understand curriculum planning and its place within their professional work. Framed through the concepts of interpretative labour and discretionary spaces, the study explores how teachers exercise professional judgement as they adapt, translate, and enact curriculum in response to particular learners and contexts. The findings suggest that teachers may not experience curriculum planning as administrative “busywork”, but as an intellectually demanding, creative, and professionally meaningful aspect of teaching. The findings highlight a tension often overlooked in workload debates: work that demands time and effort is not necessarily work that teachers wish to reduce or remove. Rather, participants described curriculum planning as a key source of professional satisfaction, agency, and connection to students’ learning. We argue that contemporary workload reduction strategies may misrecognise the nature of curriculum work by treating it as an expendable burden rather than a central dimension of professional practice. The paper concludes that addressing teacher workload requires not only reducing unnecessary administrative demands but also recognising and supporting the interpretative labour involved in curriculum making.

items.title: From Predictive Analytics to Intelligent Intervention: Integrating Causal Machine Learning, Treatment Optimization, and Decision Utility Assessment
items.abstract: Predictive accuracy does not establish that an intervention is effective. This study proposes a decision-centric artificial intelligence workflow combining predictive modelling, SHAP explainability, heterogeneous treatment-effect estimation, policy learning, and intervention-utility evaluation. Four predictive models (Logistic Regression, Random Forest, XGBoost, and LightGBM) and six causal and uplift estimators (S-Learner, T-Learner, X-Learner, LinearDML, Causal Forest, and Random Forest Two-Model Uplift) were evaluated using a treatment-balanced sample of 500,000 observations from the Criteo benchmark. Binary visit was the primary outcome, while conversion was used descriptively. XGBoost and LightGBM achieved validation AUC-ROC values of 0.94467 and 0.94455, respectively. The Spearman rank correlation between XGBoost predicted visit probabilities and Causal Forest estimated treatment effects was 0.3942 (95% bootstrap CI: 0.3873–0.4020), indicating a moderate association between predictive response and estimated incremental treatment benefit. At a 30% intervention budget, full-test-set policy values were 0.047333 for XGBoost and 0.046827 for Causal Forest, with corresponding net benefits of 0.045833 and 0.045327. In a separate 20,000-observation treatment-stratified evaluation subset, paired-bootstrap comparisons produced a Causal Forest–XGBoost policy-value difference of 0.001200 (95% CI: −0.000903 to 0.003600) and a net-benefit difference of 0.001177 (95% CI: −0.000945 to 0.003562). Neither difference was statistically distinguishable from zero. These findings demonstrate that predictive discrimination, treatment-effect ranking, and intervention utility represent distinct evaluation objectives. The results provide empirical evidence of their complementary roles within the Criteo benchmark but do not establish universal causal-policy superiority or cross-domain generalizability.

items.title: From psychological needs to knowledge practices: individual inquiry and shared learning in generative AI-supported vocational education
items.abstract: Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) provides rapid access to explanations and examples, but information access does not necessarily become effective learning. Drawing on self-determination theory, this study examined associations among autonomy, competence, and relatedness need satisfaction, knowledge acquisition, knowledge sharing, and perceived learning effectiveness. Methods A cross-sectional survey included 300 adult students in computing-related programs at seven vocational colleges in Nanchang, China. The common reference was learning in web design and development during the preceding 4 weeks. Confirmatory factor analysis and structural equation modeling were complemented by fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA). Results All three psychological needs were positively associated with knowledge acquisition. Autonomy and competence were significantly associated with knowledge sharing; the relatedness coefficient was positive but did not reach the 0.05 significance level. Acquisition and sharing were both positively associated with perceived learning effectiveness. Autonomy and competence had significant statistical indirect associations through both practices, whereas relatedness had a significant indirect association only through acquisition. These separate significance tests do not establish differences between coefficients. Three configurations were associated with high perceived effectiveness, two of which included relatedness. Low-outcome configurations remained exploratory because their proportional reduction in inconsistency values fell below the specified threshold. Discussion GenAI was the contextual framing rather than an independently measured exposure, and the knowledge practices were not exclusive to GenAI. The outcome was subjective, and neither the indirect paths nor the configurations establish causality or objective learning gains.

items.title: From safer chemistry to safer people: converging green toxicology and the human exposome
items.abstract: Chemical safety is at a crossroads. Traditional animal-based regulatory testing is increasingly challenged for its limited human relevance, high costs, ethical concerns, and inability to cope with the scale of chemical innovation. Two complementary concepts have emerged from opposite ends of the safety spectrum: Green Toxicology (GT), which integrates toxicological considerations early into chemical design to “design-out” hazards, and the Human Exposome (HE), which aims to map the totality of real-world exposures across the human life span and links them to disease burden. While developed independently, GT and HE converge on a shared technological backbone of new approach methodologies (NAMs), microphysiological systems (MPS), exposomics, artificial intelligence, and probabilistic risk assessment. GT provides the upstream leverage point of prevention, while HE offers the downstream diagnostic power of surveillance. Their fusion is proposed to create a dynamic design–monitor–redesign innovation loop, in which each candidate is evaluated prospectively during design and then monitored and re-evaluated in real-world use through exposure surveillance. This framework could strengthen regulatory confidence, support substitution without regrettable outcomes, and align with international initiatives such as REACH, TSCA reform, and OECD test guideline modernization. Beyond science and regulation, the integration could yield economic and societal dividends: potential economic benefits from shared research infrastructure, accelerated replacement of animal testing, and the advancement of environmental justice by linking safer design to exposure equity. Together, GT and HE can establish the foundation for a 21st century chemical safety paradigm that is scientifically modern, economically compelling, innovation-driving, ethically aligned, and socially just.

items.title: From Seed to BLOOM: Autonomously Growing a Better Out-of-Order Core
items.abstract: Improving microprocessor performance while meeting ASIC implementation constraints like area and frequency is a complex and labor-intensive task that requires expertise across computer architecture, hardware design, and performance analysis and profiling. While large teams in industry can afford the engineering resources to target this problem across performance modeling, RTL design, and ASIC implementations, small teams of researchers and engineers cannot take on this huge engineering burden while keeping up with the pace of advancement in processor microarchitecture. Recent advancements in large language model (LLM) agents present a promising substrate to accelerate this traditionally human-intensive process. In this work, we build and evaluate MiracleGro, an agentic AI-based system that, without human intervention, analyzes cycle-level RTL behavior and synthesis results, identifies performance bottlenecks, and translates architectural ideas into RTL implementation in a leading open-source out-of-order superscalar application core, the Berkeley Out-of-Order Machine (BOOM). Taking into account cycle-exact performance, area, and critical path, MiracleGro automatically produces improved BOOM designs that drastically increase the human-optimized BOOM's performance on substantial workload suites such as SPEC CPU2017 with full reference inputs. MiracleGro achieves an 85% IPC speedup and a frequency improvement of 27% in SkyWater 130nm, resulting in a 2.34x wall-clock time speedup on the full SPEC CPU2017 intspeed benchmarks (30 trillion instructions). This result demonstrates the enormous opportunity to harness frontier models to improve state-of-the-art RTL-driven platforms for implementation-grounded microarchitecture research across hardware designs.

items.title: From Sequence Uncertainty to Phenotype Hypotheses: Uncertainty-Conditioned Inference over Biomedical Knowledge Graphs
items.abstract: Genomic foundation models provide variant-level evidence, but connecting that evidence to phenotype hypotheses requires accounting for uncertainty throughout structured reasoning. We introduce an uncertainty-conditioned path-energy framework that converts sequence predictions and calibrated predictive uncertainty into explicit distributions over graph-supported phenotype hypotheses, without patient-level phenotype supervision. An interpretable learned energy scores admissible gene--disease--phenotype routes, query uncertainty controls the target temperature, and path probabilities are aggregated into phenotype hypotheses. This formulation makes evidence quality an explicit determinant of hypothesis breadth while retaining traceable multi-path support. Exact normalization over enumerable candidate sets provides a reference for evaluating a Hastings-corrected learned revision operator. On AlzKB and Hetionet, phenotype-level entropy tracks upstream uncertainty, with Spearman correlations of 0.951 and 0.878, respectively; ablations identify the contribution of uncertainty conditioning. In masked-edge recovery, the model exceeds chance and degree-matched probability-permutation controls. Training the energy under the uncertainty-dependent temperature yields higher held-out recall@10 than training under a constant temperature of comparable magnitude. Under gene hold-out, recall@10 exceeds that of a trained DistMult embedding on 24 of 30 graph masks (0.183 versus 0.123); this difference is attributable mainly to three genes with many variants and is not established for all genes. These results establish an uncertainty-aware interface from genomic predictions to graph-supported phenotype hypotheses that combines interpretable probability allocation with held-out association recovery of explicitly stated scope.

items.title: From Sessions to Serving: Integrating LLM-Based Embeddings into Retrieval for Production Content Recommendation
items.abstract: Personalized content recommendation on large marketplace websites must reconcile heterogeneous candidate content (e.g., customer stories, product pages, industry pages, and learning content) with sparse, fast-changing user behavior, placing increasing demands on the retrieval stage to represent user interest well, not just the downstream ranking stage. We present LSER (LLM Session Embedding Retrieval), a production content recommendation system for autodesk.com that derives session- and history-level embeddings from a pretrained large language model (LLM) and adds them as auxiliary user-side features in the retrieval-stage user tower alongside existing learned sequence encoders. To keep user-side embeddings fresh under real-time behavior, we build a nearline serving path that asynchronously refreshes sequential and LLM-derived user vectors for our main content recommendation server. We validate the incremental value of the LLM features through an ablation study across our full multi-content-type catalog. Our results indicate that integrating LLM-derived embeddings as additional retrieval signals, together with production-grade nearline serving, is technically feasible and can improve model performances.

items.title: From Shoebox to Toolbox: Archival Affirmation in the AI-Assisted Processing of a Media-Art Archive
items.abstract: Large digitised media collections often remain unprocessed and unexplored, despite being technically preserved, and archival institutions increasingly turn to artificial intelligence (AI). Rather than pursuing autonomous archival systems, this article examines how AI can support archival description and classification while preserving the contextual, historical and provenance-related integrity of archival materials. Drawing on the archive of media artist Teoman Madra (1931–2025), the study develops and evaluates an AI-assisted archival tool for a large, initially unstructured collection. The proposed approach establishes an iterative, human-in-the-loop workflow in which AI-generated suggestions are critically assessed by the archivist, whose decisions subsequently inform the system's outputs. The study shows that the controlled vocabulary given to the model shapes what it can recognise, that the archivist's validated decisions guide classification reliably within an archival unit but not across units, and that the model's contribution declines as tasks demand contextual knowledge beyond what is visible. While this process can improve efficiency and reveal details a person might miss, it also introduces epistemic risks, particularly when plausible but inaccurate classifications remain undetected. Faster processing does not by itself mean more reliable description. The article conceptualises AI-assisted archival classification as archival affirmation, a collaborative process in which human judgement remains integral to the production and validation of archival knowledge. By situating the archivist's interpretive authority at the centre of this process, the article contributes to discussions of the responsible integration, critical oversight and governance of AI in archival practice.
